scenario_constructions: Ansel Pelletier, Corinne and the sugarbush are fictional. The weather record is real NOAA data. The two start dates, the relatives' leave, the 42-day tap-hole life (MA1), the three run-day rules (MA2, MA3) and the 1996-2025 judging record (MA5) are stated scenario constructions. The decision date (January 26, 2026) is chosen so that the 2025 season is the latest complete one; the 2026 season appears only in the facilitator Twist.
sensitivity_note: SPEC 6: this case touches a family's livelihood and two relatives on unpaid leave. Frame Ansel as making a planning decision with the best record available; do not imply anyone should have known; do not ask students to imagine a specific family going without. Full note in FACILITATOR.md.

deliverables.text: A scatter plot of run days against season year, 1950-2025, under the Primary Rule, with the Early Tap and the Late Tap each as its own set of points and a line of best fit through each; one sentence per line on the direction and strength of the correlation.

For each line, a linear equation with the slope also written in run days per decade, and the season year at which the two lines meet, found by solving the two equations together; what the crossing year means and what not to trust it to say.

Under the Primary Rule, for the records 1950-1979, 1991-2020, 1996-2025, 2006-2025 and 1950-2025: mean run days for each date, the winner, the margin as a percent, and the number of seasons in which each date had more run days.

For 1991-2020, 1996-2025, 2006-2025 and 1950-2025, the means, winner and margin under each of the three rules, each rule's two slopes per decade and crossing year for 1950-2025, shown as a table or chart marking which date wins and by how much; then the rule and record the student stands on and the one cell that would reverse the pick.

balance.argument_a: Early Tap: under the rule Ansel fixed in advance, the Early Tap averages 12.67 run days against 12.07 over 1996-2025 (4.7%), ahead in 17 of 30 seasons; every record from 1976 on agrees under that rule; the fitted lines cross about 1997 with the Late Tap falling; a hard-freeze night is the defensible sap-flow stand-in.
balance.argument_b: Late Tap: it wins the whole 1950-2025 record under all three rules and the recent 30 seasons under two of the three rules (1.4% and 5.0%); the Primary Rule's 4.7% is about 1.5 standard errors of the paired gap; it wins 11 of 15 rule-by-record cells and sits near the best start date under the looser rules.
balance.margin_basis: Margin = |A-B|/larger of the two means of run days (Primary Rule, 42-day window, 1996-2025): (12.67-12.07)/12.67 = 4.7%. The winner depends on the rule and record: that dependence is the case's central finding, disclosed in FACILITATOR.md and sensitivity_disclosure[].
balance.convention: gap divided by the larger mean

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The tap-hole productive life exists physically (it varies by tree, year and hole care) but no single published figure was found after two search framings and a fetch of the Northern Woodlands page; 42 days is a good-faith scenario value from the closest public analogue (holes drilled in January can dry out by mid-April). A 50 percent shortening to 21 days flips the winner. Exception, not template; the case states the assumption in the open (MA1) and the guide says the verdict is unstable.

central_finding: The winner is a property of (rule, record), not only of the two dates: the Primary Rule gives the Early Tap 4.7% on 1996-2025, Plain Freeze-Thaw and Warm Day, Any Frost give the Late Tap 1.4% and 5.0%, and the full 1950-2025 record favors the Late Tap under all three rules.

context_glossary.desc: The building where sap is boiled down into syrup, usually with a big shallow pan over a fire.
A stand of maple trees managed for sap, the woods a sugarmaker taps.
The long shallow pan and firebox in which sap is boiled so water leaves as steam and syrup is left.
A small tube set into a drilled hole in a tree that lets sap drip or flow out into a bucket or a sap line.

context_why_notes.D1: Why a scatter plot and lines: one season is noise; the points over seventy-six years show whether either date is drifting.
context_why_notes.D2: Why equations and a crossing year: two lines cross where one date overtakes the other, and the equations make the claim checkable.
context_why_notes.D3: Why several records: the same two dates are compared on different spans of years to see how much the answer depends on the span.
context_why_notes.D4: Why a rule-by-record map: the count of run days depends on the definition, and the map shows where the answer holds and where it reverses.

context_note: Added 4 story terms (sugarhouse, sugarbush, evaporator, spout); all appear in case.md. 'tap', 'sap line' and 'unpaid leave' skipped: context explains them. No tooltip states a result. No visual added: D1 asks the student to draw the scatter plot and a pre-drawn one would pre-empt it.

math_glossary.desc: A graph of points, one for each pair of values, such as a season's year and its run days.
How closely two sets of values move together; positive when both rise together, negative when one rises as the other falls.
A straight line drawn through a scatter plot that follows the overall trend of the points.
How steep a line is: the change up or down divided by the change across.
An equation whose graph is a straight line, such as y = mx + b.
Two or more equations solved together; the answer is where their lines meet.
The sum of the values divided by how many there are.
A chart that joins points over time with a line so a trend can be seen.
